I really enjoy Incrempire. It feels different from most games I’ve played, and the overall concept is really cool. The tech tree is probably my favourite part. The upgrades are varied and give you different advantages, so sometimes it’s genuinely difficult to decide which one to buy next. Other times, I just want to click through the upgrades as quickly as possible, spend all my gold, and jump straight back into the action. It has a very satisfying gameplay loop, and I’ll definitely keep coming back to level up and see how far I can get!

This game is really addictive. Every time I finish a run, I immediately want to try again, improve my strategy, and finally beat the level. I really like how it combines survival, tower defense, and incremental progression. The skill tree always gives you something useful to work towards, and because you get stronger after every attempt, even losing does not feel like a waste of time. The game also introduces new mechanics gradually, so it never feels overwhelming. There is always something new to unlock or discover, which keeps me interested in what comes next. I already enjoy tower defense games, but Incrempire does something fresh with the genre. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes incremental, survival, or tower defense games.

Incrempire has been a pleasant surprise. If you’ve played Maktala or Slice the Crops, you’ll immediately recognize the satisfying idle progression, but Incrempire adds its own personality with a darker fantasy theme, castle upgrades, and constant unlocks that keep you chasing the next milestone. Compared to Maktala, the progression feels a bit faster early on and rewards active play without forcing you to grind endlessly. Compared to Slice the Crops, it has more variety in upgrades and a stronger sense of building an empire rather than just increasing numbers. The gameplay loop is simple but addictive: upgrade, unlock, prestige, repeat. Watching your damage and resources snowball is incredibly satisfying, and there’s always another upgrade to work toward. The art style is colorful, the animations are smooth, and it runs well. If you enjoy idle/incremental games with meaningful progression like Maktala and Slice the Crops, Incrempire is absolutely worth checking out. It’s easy to pick up for a few minutes or sink hours into without realizing it.

This is a little under half baked. Okay premise. There are only 25 levels. You will max out your skill tree before level 25, with every single node unlocked and maxed. There aren't really any builds or strategies using the skill tree. Once you beat the 25 levels (90 minutes i'd guess) there's then hard/nightmare/midnightmare modes which continue on the same exact maps, with the same enemies. The rewards are not configured correctly for hard modes (first levels will give you around 100 gold where the last level of normal mode has like 7.5mm or something), and the only changes you can make are by upgrading "runes", which are just random stat socketing items. If you are looking for something with replayability/build creativity/challenge in any way i would not recommend.

I'm not mad, I'm disappointed. This game feels lazy and deceptive. If you've played an incremental before, there's nothing here you haven't seen a million times over. The skill tree is generic, boring, and upgrade costs are [b]way[/b] out of proportion to the money you make from having to repeat the stage. The passive skills and even the towers' damage don't scale well enough, so by the end of the game they fade into background noise. The grind at the end of the game is also just insanely unfun - just fail the same mission over and over again to scrape together pennies in order to get enough upgrades to get past. Then, once you max our your skill tree, the only path forward is to upgrade runes, which are multiplicative in cost and are purely random which stats they'll buff - think Diablo item affixes. This game genuinely feels like it was padded with bad scaling and costs in order to extend playtime, but if you find an OP strat (Living Blacksmith + 3 Ore Deposits), you'll one shot most stages and you'll be done in close to 2 hours. I got to near the end but when I saw the grind ahead, I checked my playtime and found I was able to refund it, so I'm happy to do so. I honestly can't recommend this game - it feels generic, lazy, and completely uninspired.

Incrempire takes the familiar satisfaction of incremental games and wraps it in a fantasy kingdom under siege, resulting in an experience that is both relaxing and surprisingly engaging. Developed by FMGames and Regnum Noctis and published by FMGames, the title leans heavily into the "lose, improve, repeat" formula that has become a hallmark of the genre. Instead of treating failure as a setback, every defeat becomes another step toward building a stronger empire. This philosophy gives the game an addictive rhythm from the outset, encouraging players to continually push their limits while watching their kingdom grow more capable with every attempt. The game's premise is simple but effective. Players defend their castle from relentless monster invasions using a cursor-driven combat system while collecting resources to unlock permanent enhancements. At first glance, it resembles a traditional clicker game, but Incrempire introduces enough strategic considerations to elevate itself above its inspirations. The expansive skill tree allows players to customize their progression, offering upgrades that affect damage output, spell efficiency, survivability, and numerous passive bonuses. Because each upgrade contributes to long-term advancement, even brief sessions feel rewarding, creating a steady stream of accomplishments that keeps the gameplay loop compelling. Progression is where Incrempire shines the brightest. The game features five unique biomes spread across 25 stages, each introducing tougher enemies and fresh environmental themes. Temporary blessings selected at the beginning of runs provide additional variety, encouraging players to experiment with different combinations and playstyles. These roguelite-inspired mechanics help prevent repetition from setting in too quickly, especially when paired with the game's achievement system and multiple upgrade paths. While a full playthrough can be completed in a relatively short amount of time, players interested in unlocking everything and refining their strategies will likely spend many additional hours pursuing optimal builds. Visually, Incrempire adopts a colorful and approachable art direction that complements its casual nature. The battlefield remains easy to read even when enemy numbers increase dramatically, and the interface presents important information without cluttering the screen. The fantasy setting may not be particularly groundbreaking, but it is executed with enough charm to remain enjoyable throughout the experience. The soundtrack and accompanying effects further reinforce the feeling of gradual empowerment as players transform from struggling defenders into nearly unstoppable rulers. The Steam description also notes the use of AI-assisted artwork, which may divide opinions among players, though it does not significantly detract from the overall presentation. That said, Incrempire's streamlined design can occasionally work against it. Players seeking a deep strategic experience may find its mechanics somewhat limited once the initial excitement of progression begins to taper off. Enemy encounters eventually become predictable, and the lack of extensive endgame content means some players may reach the limits of what the game has to offer sooner than expected. Nevertheless, these shortcomings are tempered by the title's affordable scope and its clear understanding of its target audience. Ultimately, Incrempire succeeds by embracing accessibility and delivering a satisfying sense of growth. It doesn't attempt to redefine incremental gaming, but it executes its ideas with confidence and consistency. The combination of permanent upgrades, replayable runs, and light roguelite elements creates a gameplay loop that is easy to pick up and difficult to put down. Fans of idle and incremental titles looking for a fantasy-themed adventure with active participation will find plenty to appreciate here. Rating: 7/10
